## A biomarker that changes its mind

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
In a late-stage oncology trial, one baseline biomarker looked **unassociated
with survival**.

A standard survival model scored its effect at ≈ 0.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
sign_flip_fig()
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.0em; margin-top:-.3em;"}
**Harmful early. Protective late.** The two halves cancelled out.
:::

::: notes
OPEN HERE. Do not start with methods. Start with the curve crossing zero.
The point of the whole first act: averaging over time hid a real signal.
Pause after "the two halves cancelled out." That is the hook.

DISCLOSURE: no compound, gene, trial or variable name anywhere in this talk.
This figure is a redrawn schematic, captioned as illustrative - the study
figures could not be used because the labels are burned into the images.
If asked in Q&A: "the specific biomarker isn't something I can name here,
but the published analysis is in the reference on the last slide."

## orthoMTL: don't average over time {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
Learn **several related tasks together**, sharing strength where they agree and
staying apart where they don't.

Built first for **regression and classification**. Survival came later: cut
follow-up into **landmarks**, fit them **at once**, each keeping its own effect.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](surv_mtl.png){.fig-fit style="--fig-h:360px;" fig-alt="Diagram converting survival times into a sequence of binary classification tasks, one per landmark."}

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393; text-align:center; margin-top:-.2em;"}
Survival-as-multi-task framing after MTLSA (Li et al., KDD 2016).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.25em; margin-top:.3em;"}
**`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`** — on CRAN, 2026
:::

::: notes
This is the promotion slide. 45 seconds, no more. The sell is: if your outcome is
time-to-event and you suspect effects change over time, this package will show you that.
Vervier 2014 (method), Juric 2026 Annals of Oncology (application).
:::

## From PhD code to CRAN

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Twelve-year-old research code. An agent did the packaging work.

::: {.fragment}
Writing unit tests for the **logistic loss**, the agent found a **real bug** in
my own 2014 gradient — labels were $\pm1$, the code used the $0/1$ formula.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.4em;"}
The test it wrote: flipping every label **must** flip the answer. It didn't.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](cran.png){.fig-fit style="--fig-h:200px;" fig-alt="CRAN logo."}
:::
:::

::: notes
Keep this tight. The transferable idea is the symmetry check, not the bug.
Say: "the agent cannot invent that check — I had to know the maths. But it ran it."
:::

## Then CRAN rejected us. Twice. {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.5em; line-height:1.9; margin-top:.5em;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** An invalid `LICENSE` field.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**2.** A hard-coded `set.seed()`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.7em; color:#FF4E00;"}
Neither was caught by any automated check. Both were caught by **a CRAN volunteer**.
:::

::: notes
Deliberately dark slide, big type, slow delivery. This is the pivot from act one to act two.
Both rejections cost round-trips measured in weeks of calendar time.
CRAN is maintained by volunteers - the Repository Policy says so in its own
preamble: "CRAN is maintained by the efforts of volunteers (the CRAN team)".
Their time is described there as CRAN's most precious resource. That matters for
the argument: the scarce reviewing capacity is human and unpaid.
:::

## Would a skill file have got us there in one shot?

::: {style="font-size:1.1em;"}
An agent did the refactoring. An agent did the packaging. Then **two rounds of
human review**, on two things `R CMD check` never printed. The package is now on
CRAN — so the question is the **counterfactual**.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em;"}
Re-break the package with four defects — **no NAMESPACE**, a **LICENSE
template**, **DESCRIPTION metadata**, **unused Imports**. Hand it to an agent
under **six conditions**. Frozen prompt, fresh copy each time, results
**blinded** before scoring.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: "100%"
design_fig()
```

::: {style="font-size:.7em; margin-top:.3em; color:#939393;"}
The literature was already hedging: skills "often provide no benefit, and can
even hurt" — SkillDelta (Xu et al. 2026), SkillAxe (Gautam et al. 2026).
Skills from [posit-dev/skills](https://github.com/posit-dev/skills) and
[CoryMcCartan/agent-skills](https://github.com/CoryMcCartan/agent-skills); every
arm also had the [CRAN Cookbook](https://contributor.r-project.org/cran-cookbook/)
on disk. Full references in backup.
:::

::: notes
A4 is the cheat arm: I wrote it FROM this package's own rejection history. It should win.
Flag that now so the result lands harder.

IMPORTANT framing. Do NOT say "nobody measures skill files" - that is false and
someone in this room will know it. Skills ARE measured; the useful point is that
the measurements are already conditional, and I am adding one more condition.

SAY THIS OUT LOUD, after the hedges land - it inoculates the whole talk:
"The biggest study, SkillsBench, does find a solid average gain - but on 87
tasks hand-picked to be easier with a skill, and not one of them is R."
Then move on. One sentence, no defensiveness. If they want more, backup slide.

Be ready for the counterweight: SkillsBench (Li et al. 2026) reports +16.6 pp
across 87 tasks and is the headline positive result. If it comes up in Q&A, do
not fight it - note that its tasks are admitted only when "significantly easier
with Skills", its skills are top-quartile quality, and its software-engineering
domain gains the second-least of eight (+11.6 pp). That gradient points at my
result rather than against it. Backup slide has the detail.
:::

## Why the control did so well

::: {style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.4em;"}
::: {.fragment}
The agent runs **`R CMD check`** and reads its own failures.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em;"}
A machine oracle beats a checklist: it reflects **this** package, **today**.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Skill files add little where a tool already tells the truth.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; font-size:.92em;"}
Not unique to us: SkillFlow found agents used retrieved skills **70%** of the
time and still gained **nothing**. Reading a skill is not the same as needing one.
:::

::: {style="font-size:.78em; margin-top:.5em; color:#939393;"}
Not an argument against skill files — an argument about **where** they pay.
The CRAN rules a skill encodes are the ones `R CMD check` already enforces.
:::

::: notes
This is the mechanistic explanation and the most useful thing in the deck.

If asked "but models keep improving, so isn't the checklist point moot?" - that
cuts in my favour, not against. A better model needs the checklist less, not
more. My claim is about the tool being authoritative for this package today,
not about the checklist being stale in the abstract.

If asked "then why do people write CRAN skill files?" - three honest reasons.
(1) Most were written against weaker models, where the gap was real.
(2) They encode the part R CMD check cannot see. Our LICENSE rejection was
exactly that - and every arm fixed it, control included, so on that one the
skill file bought nothing. The set.seed rejection was also present in the
starting package, and there it was different: only the process skill (A2) and
the raw handbook (A5) mostly produced the canonical fix; the control did not.
See the backup slide; n is 9-10 per arm, so descriptive only.
(3) Writing one is cheap and feels responsible; nobody had measured whether it
works, which is why I ran this.
:::

## The part I did not expect {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.3em;"}
`R CMD check` floored because it **works**. So the judgement oracle was supposed
to see what the tool cannot.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
It had **12 criteria**. Ten never fired once.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em;"}
The two that did fire were the judge **disagreeing with itself** about text that
**no arm had touched**:
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:.92em; margin-top:.4em;"}
- the maintainer email — unchanged in all **57** runs; read as fine in 10 trees, as a problem in 47
- one sentence in the seed — flagged by 22 verdicts, *excused* by 2, and 29 never opened the file
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700; text-align:center; font-size:1.05em;"}
Both "findings" were my oracle. Not my arms.
:::

::: notes
This is the real result and I should say so plainly.

I did not find this during scoring. I found it afterwards, reading the judge's
own evidence strings - which I did not have to look at. That is the point worth
making to this audience: the failure was invisible at the summary level. The
counts looked like a clean two-criterion signal. Only the free-text justification
showed the judge arguing both sides of the same fact.

If asked "so is the whole experiment void?" - no. The machine-check result stands
on its own and is unaffected; it came from R CMD check, not the judge. What is
void is the idea that the judge panel added sensitivity on top of it.

Do not oversell this as a general claim about LLM judges. It is one package, one
rubric, one rep per tree. The transferable lesson is in the next slide.
:::

## What I am *not* claiming {.smaller}

- **Not** "skill files are useless" → where tasks are *selected* to need them, they help a lot; this is *no benefit on CRAN prep, with the docs at hand*
- **The two rejections behave differently.** The LICENSE template was repaired by every arm. The hard-coded `set.seed()` was also in the starting package, and there the arms differ (backup) — descriptive counts on 9–10 runs per arm, no test
- **N = 1** on every axis that matters: one package, one agent, one model version
- We had budget left and wanted more points, so we added 4–5 runs per arm. The N=5 results did not trigger that — we had simply costed the runs conservatively
- **No positive control**: a deliberately handicapped arm (docs removed, so a skill file is the only guidance) would have shown the measurement *can* detect a win. Without one, I can't separate "no effect" from "no sensitivity" — and the judge panel (previous slide) says the second is live
- **One open thread I can't close**: on the `set.seed()` rejection the arms *do* differ (backup). That re-score is post-unblinding, so I report it as a lead for someone else, not as support for anything above

::: notes
Say these out loud and quickly. Credibility is the currency of a null result.
Lead with the non-claim, then the reason.

The lost runs go here, orally, pointing at the arms table: 3 runs died on API
rate limits - infrastructure, not agent behaviour - so `r n_runs` of 60 are
analysed. Excluded, not rerun: a replayed run weeks later under different rate
limits is not the same experimental unit, and rerunning after unblinding would
have been the only part of this experiment scored with the labels known. Two of
the three died at 1 turn having spent $0.00, so there is no agent behaviour in
them to recover.

Say the n and the reason in the same breath as the result - do NOT bury it. The
rule is content-independent (infrastructure failures are excluded and reported,
whichever arm they hit), which is what makes a post-hoc exclusion defensible.
If I am running long this compresses to one sentence: "three runs died on rate
limits, 57 analysed, excluded not rerun." See LESSONS_LEARNED.md §11.
:::

## Postscript: the one thing every arm agreed on {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: {style="font-size:1.12em; margin-top:.3em;"}
The judge flagged **one** criterion in almost every tree — our own maintainer
address:

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.4em;"}
`kevin.vervier@novartis.com`
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em;"}
CRAN requires **a person, not a mailing list**, kept current and reachable
"**without any form of filtering**". A corporate account is one re-org away
from failing all three.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700; text-align:center;"}
Not a violation today. Changing in **0.2.0** anyway.
:::

::: notes
The laugh line, and it must be told precisely or someone will correct me.

It is NOT currently against the rules - a named person at a company address is
compliant. The exposure is filtering and job changes, both anticipated by the
policy language. Say "not a violation today" out loud; do not oversell it.

Do NOT say "a newer model spotted this". It is criterion C13, it was in the
corpus from the start, and the judge flagged it in 47 of the 57 analysed trees -
the experiment found it, which is the better story anyway: the thing nearly all
six conditions agreed on was the one defect I had shipped to CRAN myself.

Precision point (corrected 2026-10-07): do NOT say "every arm except A5". No arm
ever changed the address - it is still kevin.vervier@novartis.com in all 57 runs.
The 10 COMPLIANT verdicts (7 of them A5) are the judge excusing the corporate
domain because Novartis Pharma AG is also the listed copyright holder. That is
judge variance on an under-specified criterion, not an arm fixing anything. If
asked about the A5 column in the results table, say that.
:::

## Take home {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: {style="font-size:1.05em; line-height:1.45;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** Learning related tasks **jointly or separately** is the general tool;
survival is its most recent use case → `orthoMTL`
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.35em;"}
**2.** Agents are good at checks a **machine** can run. Invest in **executable
oracles** — tests, `R CMD check`, symmetry checks — before prose guidance.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.35em;"}
**3.** I set out to measure skill files. I couldn't — my judge measured itself.
Finding out **why** was worth more than the answer.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; text-align:center; font-size:1.15em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Generation got cheap. Verification did not.
:::

::: notes
Point 3 replaced the label-flip line, which now lives in the correctness backup.
The three points are meant to escalate: the science, the practical advice, the
thing that cost me a month to learn.

Land the closing line slowly. It is the thesis of the whole talk, not a sign-off -
the experiment is the evidence for it. If I only get one sentence remembered,
this is the one.
:::

::: {style="font-size:.55em; margin-top:.3em; text-align:center;"}
[`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`](https://github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL) · Vervier et al. 2014 · Juric et al. 2026 · full references in backup
:::

## Backup: the hedges, in their own words {.smaller}

| Finding | Source |
|:--|:--|
| Skills "often provide no benefit, and can even hurt performance while incurring additional token costs" | SkillDelta, Xu et al. 2026 |
| Human-authored skills +16.2 pp; **LLM-authored skills give no measurable gain** | SkillAxe, Gautam et al. 2026 |
| Agents used retrieved skills 70% of the time yet showed **no performance gain** where the corpus lacked good skills for the domain | SkillFlow, Li et al. 2026 |
| Self-generated skills landed **below** the no-skills baseline (−8 to −11.5 pp) | SkillsBench, Li et al. 2026 |

My null is the same shape, in a domain none of them covered.

## Backup: the counterweight {.smaller}

The headline positive result is **SkillsBench**: curated skills lift pass rate
33.9% → 50.5% (**+16.6 pp**) across 87 tasks and 18 model–harness configurations.
I am not disputing it. Three things make it a different question from mine:

- **8 domains** — natural science, media, cybersecurity, industrial, finance, office, software engineering, maths/OR. **No R, no packaging, no CRAN**
- Tasks are admitted only if **"significantly easier with Skills"**; no-separation tasks are rejected as low-signal
- Skills are drawn from the **top quality quartile** (10.1/12 vs ecosystem mean 6.2/12); the authors call this "an optimistic scenario"

Their own domain gradient points my way: **software engineering +11.6 pp**,
second-lowest of eight, against natural science **+28.8 pp** — "domains with
stronger pretraining and tooling coverage benefit less."

::: notes
Use this slide only if challenged. The honest summary: SkillsBench asks "how much
can a good skill help where a skill should help?" I ask "did a skill help on the
job I actually had?" My four defects were not chosen for skill-dependence, and
three of four are machine-detectable. The two results bracket the same effect
from opposite ends rather than conflicting.
:::

## Backup: the three ways we checked correctness {.smaller}

| Check | What it proves |
|:--|:--|
| Against the old validated package | identical coefficients on 5 fixed cases |
| Flip every label | answer must flip; `0.62` → `0.000` |
| Simulated data, known truth | recovers the right features, 10/10 seeds |

::: notes
The survival path is exactly where comparing against the old code cannot reach —
there was no old survival code. That is why the simulation oracle exists.
:::

## Backup: cost per run

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
```

## Backup: what I would change

- Score **R01, the `set.seed()` finding**, with a rule that also sees seeds passed as default arguments, and add judge-side defects so the judge can discriminate
- Seed more defects only a **CRAN volunteer** could catch
- Add a **positive control**: an arm with the CRAN docs removed, so the skill file is the only guidance. If that arm does worse, the measurement has teeth
- Judge each package several times, not once
- More packages, more models

## Backup: the four seeded defects {.smaller}

| Defect | Caught by `R CMD check`? | Repaired |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `NAMESPACE` deleted | yes — check cannot even run | 57/57 |
| `usethis` LICENSE template vs GPL-3 DESCRIPTION | **no** — this is rejection **R02** | **57/57** |
| DESCRIPTION metadata (`Authors@R`, title case) | yes | 57/57 |
| Unused declared `Imports` | yes | 57/57 |

Three of four are machine-visible. Our other real rejection — **R01, the
hard-coded `set.seed()`** — is a fifth defect that `R CMD check` does not report;
it is on the next slide.

Three of four machine-visible is the result's main caveat: this measures the
easy half of CRAN preparation.

## Backup: the hard-coded seed (R01) {.smaller}

The starting package defaulted `seed = 42` and called `set.seed()` unconditionally in
four exported functions — the exact pattern CRAN rejected. `R CMD check` does not report it.

| Arm | n | Still hard-coded | Default kept, RNG state restored | Canonical fix (`seed = NULL`) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| A0 control | 10 | 6 | 4 | 0 |
| A1 checklist | 9 | 1 | 8 | 0 |
| A2 process | 9 | 1 | 1 | 7 |
| A3 general R | 10 | 3 | 7 | 0 |
| A4 oracle* | 10 | 4 | 6 | 0 |
| A5 raw handbook | 9 | 1 | 0 | 8 |

Completed runs only; descriptive counts, no test. "Default kept" means `seed = 42` stays but the
value goes through a helper that restores the user's RNG state — arguably acceptable, not what the
reviewer asked for. \*A4 is an upper bound, not a competitor.

**These counts are a re-score, run after unblinding.** My original rule only matched
`set.seed(<literal>)` inside a function body, so it scored **zero hits on the seed itself** — a
detector that cannot see the defect it was built for. I found that while preparing this talk, fixed
the rule, and re-ran it. The re-score reads package files only and never touches the blind map: the
same code at first unblinding would have produced this same table. The flaw was in the detector, not
in the direction of the correction.

::: notes
Be upfront - I seeded what I could verify automatically, which is exactly the
half where the control was always going to do well. The honest version of this
experiment seeds the other half, and that is the first thing I would change.

On the post-unblinding point, say it before anyone asks, and say it in this order:
(1) the rule was wrong, (2) here is how it was wrong, (3) it is a pure function of
tree content, so the timing cannot have biased the direction. rescore_r01.R takes
a tree path and returns hits; it has no access to arm labels. Validated on 8
synthetic cases, the seed (3 hits), baseline and control (0), and a mutant (1).

I am NOT claiming this as a skill-file win. Two things block that. It is one
criterion at n=9-10 with no test, and A4 - the arm written from this exact
rejection history - produced the canonical fix zero times, which is the opposite
of what a clean skill effect looks like. Report it as the most interesting loose
end in the dataset and move on.

If asked why A2 and A5 and nobody else: the cookbook contains the canonical
seed = NULL pattern verbatim, in a section every arm could read. A5 had that text
front-loaded into context rather than pointed at; A2 is the adversarial-review
arm. That is a hypothesis about front-loading vs distillation, not a finding.
:::
